recent_posts.title: Running a Computer Without RAM
recent_posts.summary: An exploration of running a computer with minimal or no RAM. Starting with Linux swap files on SATA SSD and VRAM (via a FUSE filesystem over OpenCL), the experiment shows severe performance degradation. The deeper dive covers CPU cache-as-RAM using the open-source CoreBoot firmware: by intercepting CoreBoot's early initialization stage, a small program (a Snake game) runs entirely in CPU cache on a 2009 ASRock motherboard with no RAM sticks installed, outputting via serial port. The experiment reveals that the CPU on that board doesn't cache ROM, so it reads instructions directly from BIOS flash, explaining the poor performance.

recent_posts.title: Building a universal file converter that runs entirely in your browser
recent_posts.summary: A developer built a browser-based file converter that works entirely locally, converting between any file formats including cross-medium conversions (like video to PDF or images to audio). The project uses WebAssembly ports of FFmpeg and ImageMagick, custom-built Office document parsers, and clever algorithms like Fourier transforms for audio-to-image conversion. The system uses breadth-first search to chain conversion tools together, routing through intermediate formats to reach any target format. All processing happens client-side for privacy, with lazy-loading to reduce initial bundle size.

recent_posts.title: The Programming of your Favorite Flash Games
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into the technical implementation of classic Flash games through code decompilation. Examines "Sugar, sugar"'s pixel-based collision detection using color values, "Portal: The Flash Version"'s simplified portal mechanics with hard-coded cardinal directions, "Run"'s fake 3D rendering using 2D shape projection before Flash 10's native 3D support, and "Interactive Buddy"'s custom physics engine and Turing-complete scripting language. Reveals common patterns like spaghetti code, duplicated logic, and clever workarounds that made these games run on 2011-era hardware.

recent_posts.title: Building a minecraft world mapped to your file system
recent_posts.summary: A developer creates a custom Minecraft world where every block represents a file on their computer, with breaking blocks deleting the corresponding files. The project involves building a custom level data parser, implementing terrain generation algorithms that map file system structure to island layouts, and creating a system to detect block destruction and delete files in real-time. Testing on Linux and Windows virtual machines demonstrates how breaking blocks can progressively damage the operating system, with Linux proving more vulnerable than Windows due to its leaner architecture.

recent_posts.title: Monitoring computer activity through acoustic analysis of hardware components
recent_posts.summary: Computer hardware components produce distinct acoustic signatures that can be analyzed to monitor system activity. Hard drive seek operations create clicking sounds detectable via spectrogram analysis, while GPU and power supply inductor coils emit high-frequency noise correlated with rendering workload. A custom program demonstrates using microphone input to predict GPU utilization from these acoustic patterns.

recent_posts.title: Extracting computer activity through acoustic and optical side channels
recent_posts.summary: An experimental investigation into side-channel attacks on consumer computers, examining whether system activity can be determined through acoustic and optical signals. Tests include analyzing CPU fan noise, hard drive sounds, GPU coil whine, and Ethernet LED patterns to estimate workload and network activity. While some correlations exist (particularly with GPU coil whine and network LEDs), most methods prove unreliable for personal computers due to environmental factors and hardware limitations. Demonstrates data transmission through artificial LED modulation as a proof of concept.

recent_posts.title: Building a minecraft server on a $1 microcontroller
recent_posts.summary: A developer created a fully functional Minecraft server running on a $1 ESP32-C3 microcontroller with only 300KB of memory. The project required writing a custom server from scratch in C, implementing clever optimizations like bilinear interpolation for terrain generation, mirrored cave systems, and grid-based biomes. Despite significant compromises including no anti-cheat, instant liquid flow, and simplified crafting mechanics, the server successfully supports multiple players with infinite world generation.
